_comment: Everything you own that no bank reports: the home, the cars — and the loans against them. The refresh job reads this file; the app never does. Each item is anchored to a value you know on a date you know, and then moved forward by a method you choose. Nothing here is guessed for you: an item with no usable method holds its anchor value and the app says so. WHAT SHIPS HERE IS AN EXAMPLE HOUSEHOLD, invented by scripts/make_demo_finances.py — round anchor figures, no address, nobody's car. Replace every line with your own before the first real run.

_methods.ssb-bolig: Indexed by Statistics Norway's used-dwelling price index (table 07221, quarterly, open API, no key). Needs `region` and `dwellingType`, matched by name against what the table offers — run `python3 scripts/finances.py --probe-assets` to list them. This is the honest one where it applies: it moves with the market that actually sets the price, and its history goes back to 1992, so past net worth is real rather than a flat line. It is a NORWEGIAN index. Outside Norway either point `method` at `rate` with an assumption you can defend, or swap in your own country's published index — the shape the code needs is a date-to-level series, and `ssb_series()` in scripts/finances.py is the one function to replace.
_methods.rate: A fixed annual percentage, compounded daily. For anything with no published index — a holiday property in a thin market, a boat, or a home anywhere the index above does not cover. Say what the rate is based on in `note`; it is your assumption, not a measurement.
_methods.depreciation: A retention curve by age, for vehicles. `curve` is a list of [years, share of value remaining]; beyond the last point it continues at `tailRate` per year, with `floor` as the scrap value it never goes below. Value = anchorValue x curve(age now) / curve(age at anchor), so anchoring at what you actually paid keeps the model honest about your particular car.
_methods.fixed: Holds the anchor value. For things that do not drift, or where you would rather type a number now and then than model it.

assets.name: Home
assets._anchor: What it was worth on anchorDate — a valuation, a purchase price, or the tax assessment. Everything after this is indexed off it, so a bad anchor is a bad line.
assets._variants: The valuation bases the app offers behind a switch. THE FIRST ONE IS WHAT NET WORTH IS BUILT FROM — the `region` and `dwellingType` above are only used when this list is empty — and the rest ride along so the app can redraw without fetching anything. They exist because more than one cut of the index is defensible for the same home: the whole market, or your own dwelling type, or your own town. Which one you believe is yours to pick. Anything you add here is fetched too: region and dwellingType take the same names as `--probe-assets` lists.
assets.note: Example text — a round figure on a round date, not a valuation of anything

assets.name: Estate car
assets._anchorValue: Not a purchase price: a round figure for a three-year-old estate. Replace it with what you actually paid, set anchorDate to when you bought it, and the curve becomes honest about your car rather than about the model.
assets._curve: Roughly 20 % gone after a year, 30 % after two, 40 % after three, then settling to about 10 % a year from age six. Replace with your own points if you know the model holds its value differently.

_loans: Modelled from the terms, because PSD2 covers payment accounts and a mortgage usually is not one. If your bank DOES expose the loan, it turns up as an ordinary account with a negative balance and that real figure wins — set `preferBankBalance` to the account name and the model is only used until it appears. `kind` is "annuity" (equal total payment) or "serial" (equal principal).
_floatingRate: If these are floating-rate loans, `nominalRate` is only true until the bank changes it, and the modelled balance drifts away from the real one. The cure is to update `nominalRate` when the bank writes to you, and to re-anchor `principal` and `startDate` to a balance you have read off yourself if the drift gets wide.
